newsitem.title: USA: CFTC promises swift action on CBOT delivery terms.
newsitem.headline: CFTC promises swift action on CBOT delivery terms.

text.p: The head of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said on Tuesday the agency will move swiftly to finalize delivery changes for the corn and soybean futures contracts after a public hearing next week.

The CFTC has scheduled a rare public hearing on June 12 for the Chicago Board of Trade to defend its proposed delivery terms, which would eliminate the ports of Toledo and St. Louis in favor of the northern Illinois River.

"I would like to proceed as swiftly as we can," CFTC head Brooksley Born told reporters after a speech to the National Cotton Council. "I think it would be useful to have certainty as to what the delivery provisions of the corn and bean contracts will be in the future."

The proposal has been one of the most controversial in CFTC history, igniting criticism from the governor of Ohio, Ohio Senator John Glenn, Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar and dozens of farm groups.
The public comment period for the proposal ends June 16, and the agency has already received more than 400 letters, mostly in opposition to the CBOT proposal.
Futures regulators would not be influenced by the sheer volume of comments flooding into the agency, she said.
"This is not a popularity contest. It is an issue of whether the CBOT proposal meets the statutory requirements that we are mandated to uphold," Born said.
If the CFTC decides to reject the delivery changes proposed by the CBOT, the agency has the right to publish its own proposed changes in the Federal Register. "That's under consideration," Born said.
Regulators asked the CBOT in 1995 to propose changes in the delivery terms of the big corn and soybean contracts to reflect dwindling warehouse storage facilities in Chicago.
Born also said that discussions were continuing among the CFTC, the major U.S. futures exchanges and other industry groups toward reaching a compromise proposal on legislative reform of the agency.
"I think that various participants in the discussion are moving closer together," Born said.

The Senate Agriculture committee had planned to hold a mark-up last month on proposed legislation that would strip the CFTC of most of its regulatory authority over futures traders. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and dozens of farm groups have criticized the proposed legislation as leaving the U.S. futures markets vulnerable to manipulation.
Similar legislation has been introduced in the House.
